hook.text: A handbag priced at $500 sold poorly. The company raised the price to $2,000. Sales tripled.

buildup.text: Veblen goods violate the law of demand. Price increases boost demand because the high price is the product's appeal.

discovery.text: The effect exists because status is relative. If everyone can afford it, it stops signaling exclusivity.

twist.text: Discount luxury brands fail because they undermine the signal. A cheap Rolex would destroy the brand faster than bad.

climax.text: When you desire an expensive item, ask: do I want the product or the price tag? The answer reveals the true purchase.

punchline.text: When the price is the product, economics runs backward.

quiz.question: What are Veblen goods?
options: Goods whose demand drops when price increases
Goods whose demand rises when price increases due to status signaling
Goods that are only available through government auctions

details.summary: The Veblen effect occurs when demand for a good increases as its price rises because the high price itself confers status. These goods violate the standard law of demand, with their social signaling value increasing proportionally to their costliness.
details.whyItMatters: The Veblen effect explains the billion-dollar luxury goods industry. Brands like Rolex and Hermès would lose value if they became affordable because their economic function is signaling wealth, not telling time or carrying things.
takeaways: Higher prices can increase demand by enhancing social signaling value
The Veblen effect violates the fundamental law of demand
Luxury brands deliberately maintain high prices to preserve status value

faq.question: What distinguishes Veblen goods from normal luxury goods?
faq.answer: Normal luxury goods have high demand despite high prices due to quality. Veblen goods have high demand because of high prices. Lowering the price of a Veblen good would actually decrease demand by destroying its status signaling function.

faq.question: Are Veblen goods only physical products?
faq.answer: No. Exclusive memberships, elite university tuition, premium event tickets, and even high consultant fees can exhibit Veblen effects. Any good or service where the high price itself is part of the value proposition can function as a Veblen good.
